etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English aloud, a loude (“aloud”), equivalent to a- +‎ loud or a- +‎ loude (“sound”).

definitions.definition: With a loud voice, or great noise; loudly; audibly.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter V, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: Then we relapsed into a discomfited silence, and wished we were anywhere else. But Miss Thorn relieved the situation by laughing aloud, and with such a hearty enjoyment that instead of getting angry and more mortified we began to laugh ourselves, and instantly felt better.

quote.citation: 1921, Ben Travers, chapter 1, in A Cuckoo in the Nest, Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, Page & Company, published 1925, →OCLC:
quote.text: He read the letter aloud. Sophia listened with the studied air of one for whom, even in these days, a title possessed some surreptitious allurement.

quote.citation: 2004, James Anderson, The Art of God, page 176:
quote.text: When you are meditating with sound, it can be aloud or it can be silent
